subject: backend
question: Is it true that orders are cancelled only when a user deliberately clicks the Cancel link?
ai_claim: Yes. The endpoint runs only when its URL is requested, and the only way to request it is to click the link.

ai_solution.text: cancel_order runs when /orders/{id}/cancel is requested.
The link is shown on the order page.
Only a user clicking the link sends that request.
So orders are cancelled only on purpose.

failure.misconception: Assuming only people follow GET links
failure.explanation: GET is defined as a safe method, and software relies on that: browsers prefetch and prerender links, link-preview bots and security scanners in email and chat fetch URLs, and extensions crawl pages. Any of them can request /orders/42/cancel with the user's cookies and cancel the order. State changes belong behind POST (or DELETE) with a form or fetch call.
failure.why_convincing: In manual testing, nothing ever requests the URL except the tester's click.

canonical_solution: No: prefetchers, previewers and crawlers issue GET requests freely because GET is supposed to be safe. Make cancellation a POST.

valid_evidence.summary: RFC 9110: GET is a safe method; clients may issue it without the user intending any state change.
A chat app's link preview fetches /orders/42/cancel with the user's session and cancels the order.

counterexamples: A browser prefetch of the link cancels the order.

hints.text: List everything that can make a GET request to a URL.
Step 3 assumes only a human click requests the URL.
HTTP defines GET as safe, so browsers and bots request GET URLs without asking.
Consider link previews and browser prefetching.
Step 3 is wrong: automated clients follow GET links freely. Use POST for state changes.

repair: Change the route to `@app.post("/orders/{order_id}/cancel")` and trigger it from a form or fetch.
debrief: HTTP method semantics are a contract that the whole web depends on. Browsers, caches and crawlers treat GET as harmless; an endpoint that breaks the contract will eventually be triggered by something that trusted it.

subject: backend
question: Can a client detect a missing user by checking response.ok, as most HTTP clients do?
ai_claim: Yes. The endpoint reports the error, so the client sees it as a failed request when it checks response.ok.

ai_solution.text: When the user does not exist, the endpoint returns an error message.
The response describes the failure.
Clients check response.ok to detect failures.
So a missing user shows up as a failed request.

failure.misconception: Reporting failure in the body but success in the status
failure.explanation: The endpoint returns status 200, so response.ok is true and generic tooling - HTTP clients, retries, monitoring, caches - treats it as success. Only code that parses the body and looks for an error field notices. Return 404 with the error body.
failure.why_convincing: The body clearly says 'error', so it seems the failure has been reported.

canonical_solution: No: the status is 200, so response.ok is true. Raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail='user not found').

valid_evidence.summary: GET /users/999 returns status 200 with body {"error": "user not found"}; response.ok is true.
HTTP status codes signal the outcome; 404 Not Found indicates a missing resource.

counterexamples: Monitoring counts every missing-user request as a success.

hints.text: Check the status code of the error response.
Step 2 says the response 'describes the failure'. Where?
Clients and infrastructure read the status code, not the body, to decide success.
Request a user that does not exist and inspect response.ok.
Step 2 is wrong: the failure is only in the body; the status is 200. Return 404.

debrief: The status code is the machine-readable outcome of an HTTP request. Errors inside 200 responses defeat every generic tool that understands HTTP, from fetch to load balancers.

subject: backend
question: Will old clients' POST requests, with their JSON body, be re-sent to /api/v2/orders as POSTs?
ai_claim: Yes. A redirect tells the client to repeat the request at the new URL, so the POST and its body go to /api/v2/orders.

ai_solution.text: The client POSTs an order to /api/v1/orders.
The server responds 301 with Location: /api/v2/orders.
The client repeats the same request at the new location.
So the order is created by v2.

failure.misconception: Forgetting that 301 and 302 allow a method change
failure.explanation: For historical reasons, clients may - and browsers and many libraries do - change POST to GET when following 301 or 302, dropping the body. The order becomes a GET /api/v2/orders, which lists orders or fails. 307 and 308 require the method and body to be preserved; use 308 for a permanent move.
failure.why_convincing: Redirects 'send you to the new URL', and for GET requests that is exactly what happens.

canonical_solution: No: on 301 many clients switch to GET without the body. Use 308 Permanent Redirect (or 307) to preserve the method.

valid_evidence.summary: RFC 9110: for 301 and 302, a user agent may change POST to GET; 307 and 308 forbid changing the method.
fetch('/api/v1/orders', { method: 'POST', body }) follows the 301 with GET /api/v2/orders.

counterexamples: Browsers convert the redirected POST into a GET with no body.

hints.text: Check which redirect codes preserve the method.
Step 3 assumes the client repeats the request unchanged.
301 and 302 permit changing POST to GET; 307 and 308 do not.
Follow the redirect with fetch and watch the method.
Step 3 is wrong: after 301, POST typically becomes GET. Use 308.

debrief: Redirect codes differ in two ways: permanent versus temporary, and whether the method may change. For APIs that receive POST, PUT or DELETE, only 307 and 308 are safe.

subject: backend
question: Does this CORS configuration prevent anyone except the shop's own frontend from calling /admin/refund?
ai_claim: Yes. CORS allows only https://shop.example, so requests from any other origin or client are rejected.

ai_solution.text: CORS lists the origins allowed to call the API.
Only https://shop.example is allowed.
Requests from other origins or tools are rejected by the server.
So only the shop frontend can issue refunds.

failure.misconception: Using CORS as an authorisation mechanism
failure.explanation: CORS is enforced by browsers, and it only controls whether a page on another origin may read the response. The server still receives and executes every request. curl, scripts, mobile apps and backend services ignore CORS entirely, so anyone can POST /admin/refund. The endpoint needs authentication and an authorisation check.
failure.why_convincing: In the browser, a page on another site does see a CORS error, which looks like a rejection.

canonical_solution: No: CORS does not stop non-browser clients, and even cross-site browser requests may reach the server. Add authentication and an admin check.

valid_evidence.summary: curl -X POST https://api.shop.example/admin/refund?order_id=7 succeeds; curl ignores CORS.
CORS is a browser mechanism for relaxing the same-origin policy; it is not server-side access control.

counterexamples: A curl request issues a refund.

hints.text: Ask who enforces CORS.
Step 3 says the server rejects requests from other clients.
Browsers enforce CORS by withholding responses; servers still process requests.
Call the endpoint with curl.
Step 3 is wrong: CORS is enforced by browsers only. Add authentication and authorisation.

repair: Require an authenticated admin user on the endpoint; treat CORS only as a browser read policy.
debrief: CORS protects users' browsers from other sites reading your API's responses with their credentials. It does nothing to protect the API from anyone who is not using a browser. Authorisation belongs in the endpoint.

subject: backend
question: Is the AI right that a client re-requesting an unchanged catalog, with the ETag it received earlier, gets a 304 with no body and reuses its cached copy?
ai_claim: Yes. The client sends If-None-Match with its ETag; if the catalog is unchanged the hashes match, so the server returns 304 Not Modified without a body and the client uses its cached copy.

ai_solution.text: The first response includes an ETag, the hash of the catalog.
On the next request the client sends If-None-Match with that value.
If the catalog has not changed, the hashes are equal and the server returns 304 with no body.
The client reuses its cached response; a changed catalog produces a new ETag and a full 200.

canonical_solution: Correct. This is HTTP revalidation: the ETag identifies the representation, and 304 tells the client its copy is current, saving the transfer. (A full implementation would also handle weak ETags and lists of ETags.)

valid_evidence.summary: Second request with If-None-Match equal to the ETag returns 304 and an empty body.
RFC 9110: 304 Not Modified has no content; the client uses its stored response.

hints.text: Follow the ETag through both requests.
Step 3 depends on the ETag changing only when the catalog changes.
A content hash as ETag plus If-None-Match lets the server confirm the client's copy is current.
Make two requests and compare statuses.
This solution is correct. Matching ETags produce a 304 with no body, and the client reuses its copy. The right judgment was to approve it.

debrief: Conditional requests make caching correct: the client may keep a copy, but checks it cheaply. Content-hash ETags change exactly when the representation changes, which is what makes this implementation sound.
